newsitem.title: CHILE: COPPER - Codelco sees flat production costs.
newsitem.headline: COPPER - Codelco sees flat production costs.

text.p: Chilean state copper company Codelco expects no real improvement in its production costs on a per-pound basis next year, but temporarily halting a trend toward lower costs, new CEO Marcos Lima said in an interview.
Codelco's largest mine, Chuquicamata, made up in September all ground lost in May's 10-day strike and could produce about 630,000 tonnes of copper this year, Lima said.
Drilling at the San Antonio deposit, one of Codelco's most promising new tracts, had shown the area contained less copper than the 100,000-tonnes-a-year once expected, he said.
"It is not a world-class deposit," he said of San Antonio. "There had originally been talk of 100,000 tonnes a year and, in accordance with our studies, we realize it's not going to be like that."

The San Antonio deposit in northern Chile's Third Region has been seen in Codelco as a good prospect for investment by Chilean pension funds, which have long been eager to gain a stake in the copper business.
"This doesn't mean we're not going to put together a project with the pension funds," he said. "But there's probably less copper there than we expected at the beginning."
More precise statistics on the deposit's volume and grade await further exploration, he said.
Lima said the company's cash cost will stay roughly even next year at 48 cents for every pound of copper produced.
"1997 is going to be a difficult year. We can't promise a substantial lowering in our cash cost. Maybe one cent, but we're not going to get much more than that," he said.

A company's cash cost is seen as a barometer of its efficiency and ability to withstand price fluctuations. Codelco has been gradually cutting its costs from 59 cents in 1994 but is still on the high end in the mining industry.

Lima, who took over from Juan Villarzu as CEO in September, said Codelco will produce 1.4 billion to 1.5 billion tonnes of copper a year by 1999, with output from the new Radomiro Tomic mine near Chuquicamata and expansion at the Andina mine.
Radomiro Tomic is on target to come on stream in early 1998 at 150,000 tonnes a year, becoming "the first large copper mine ever built from zero by Chileans," he said.
The Andina expansion has already begun kicking in and will raise that mine's production to 200,000 tonnes by 1999, Codelco officials have said.

Both projects are being paid for by Codelco's own funds, said Lima. A $500 million syndicated loan from a group of North American, European and Japanese banks signed this week will go mainly toward shifting short-term loans into the long-term category to ease repayment terms, he said.

Codelco is negotiating more joint venture agreements with private mining concerns, like that with Cyprus Amax Minerals at El Abra and one with Homestake Mining at the Agua de la Falda gold deposit, said Lima.
But it needs to find deposits rich enough to attract strategic partners, he said.
